1.goal: To open on the questions she gets in her real meetings, and to tell her what the lesson ends with.
1.interaction: T–S, spoken. One open question; Portuguese is fine for a word she does not have.
run: Ask whether she opened the pre-class, and whether she wrote notes for an update.
Tell her what the lesson ends with, in one sentence: she gives her own update in a team meeting and answers questions.
Ask the question on screen and take one answer.
exact: What today is: “Today you give an update on your work in a team meeting, and you answer questions about it.”
If she answers in general terms: “Think of the last meeting. What did someone ask you?”
1.expected: One or two kinds of questions from her real meetings, for example “When it will be ready” or “Why the numbers changed”. Any answer is useful: it tells you which questions to ask on screens 8 and 9 if she chooses option B.
1.support: If she cannot think of one, offer two: questions about dates, or questions about numbers.
1.challenge: Ask which question is the hardest for her to answer, and why.
1.monitoring: Whether she describes real meetings in more detail than in lesson 1.
1.evidence: The kinds of questions she gets in her meetings, in her words.
1.transition: Move on when she has named one kind of question.

2.goal: To establish her role, who is listening, what can happen, and what the update has to achieve.
2.interaction: T–S, reading the brief on screen together.
run: Read the brief with her.
Ask the question on screen and let her answer in one sentence.
2.expected: Something close to “Where my work is, what comes next, and what I need.” The last line of the brief gives it: “The team knows where your work is, what comes next, and what you need.”
2.support: If she answers with details of a project, point at “What you want by the end” and read it with her.
2.challenge: Ask what makes a question difficult in a check-in.
2.monitoring: Whether she can say the goal of the update in one sentence.
2.evidence: Her sentence about what the team needs.
2.transition: Move on when she has said what the team needs.

3.goal: To hear her update before any model, with two follow-up questions, so the lesson can compare it with the update at the end.
3.interaction: T–S. She gives the update; you listen, ask two questions, and write.
run: Read the two options with her and let her choose. With option B, ask what the work is in one sentence.
Give her a moment to look at her notes, if she has them. Then let her give the update without interruption.
Write down her update as close to word for word as you can. It goes into the third box on screen 10.
Ask the two questions below. Leave corrections and help for later: this is her first attempt.
exact: Option A, question 1: “Is the system on all the laptops?” Question 2: “When will the last laptop be ready?”
Option B, question 1: “Is it on track?” Question 2: “When will it be finished?”
3.expected: There is no key: this is her first attempt. What you are looking for is which of the three parts appear (status, next step, what she needs) and what she does with the second question, which may not have an answer. For option A, the facts are on the screen: the laptops are here, nineteen work, one has a problem with the screen. A reply like “I don't know” to the second question is useful evidence, not a mistake to correct now.
3.support: If she stops completely, read the first question on screen: “Where is the work now?”
3.challenge: Ask a third question about something she needs from the team.
3.monitoring: Which parts appear, how long the update is, and what she does when she does not know an answer.
3.evidence: Her first update, written down, and her reply to the second question.
3.transition: Move on when she has given the update and answered the two questions.

4.goal: To compare her update with a model, and to find the part that was missing in hers.
run: Play the five sentences once.
Ask the questions on screen: which parts were also in her update, and which part was not.
Play again if she asks, and point at each sentence as she compares.
exact: Before pressing Play: “Listen to your colleague. Then tell me: what did your colleague say that you did not say?”
4.expected: The model has five parts: where the work is (“On my side, the new system is on the laptops.”), the detail with the problem (“Nineteen laptops are working, but one still has a problem with the screen.”), the next step (“The next step is to get a new laptop from the supplier.”), what she needs (“I need Ryan to call the supplier this week.”) and what to say when she does not know (“About the date, I am not sure yet. I will check and get back to you.”). The part most often missing in a first update is what she needs, or the reply for a question without an answer.
4.support: Go sentence by sentence and ask: did you say something like this?
4.challenge: Ask which sentence from the model she would change for her own work.
4.monitoring: Whether she can compare her update with the model, part by part.
4.evidence: The part she says was missing in her update.
4.transition: Move on when she has named the part that was missing.

5.goal: To separate replies that keep a meeting moving from replies that stop it, when the answer is not known.
5.interaction: S says her answers and you mark them on screen, then T–S to check.
run: Read Paula's question with her.
For each of the six replies, she says the answer and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through them out loud. On each reply that stops the meeting, ask what Paula has to do next.
exact: On a reply that stops the meeting: “After this reply, what does Paula have to do?”
5.expected: The meeting keeps moving: “I am not sure yet. I will check with the supplier and tell you today.” · “I do not have the date now. Can I send it to you after the meeting?” · “Good question. Let me check with Ryan and get back to you by the end of the day.” The meeting stops: “I don't know.” · “Maybe Tuesday. Or Friday. I am not sure.” · “That is not my problem.” The one people often place in the wrong group is the reply with two days: it sounds like an answer, and Paula still cannot plan with it.
5.support: On each reply, ask: after this, does Paula know what happens next?
5.challenge: Ask her to change “I don't know.” into a reply that keeps the meeting moving.
5.monitoring: Whether she sees the difference between a guess and a next step.
5.evidence: Which replies she placed in the other group.
5.transition: Move on when the six are sorted.

6.goal: To have her find what the good replies give, and to show the parts of a short update after her answer.
run: Read the two replies with her and ask the question on screen.
Let her answer before you open the button.
Open it and read it with her. Ask her for one reply of her own for a question from her real meetings, from screen 1.
exact: If she does not see it: “Does Paula get the date? What does she get?”
Asking for her own reply: “Someone asks you a question you cannot answer. What do you say?”
6.expected: The two replies give Paula what she will do and when: check with the supplier and tell her today; send the date after the meeting. From the reveal: “On my side, …” — where your work is; “The next step is …” — what comes next; “I need …” — what you need and from whom; “I will check and get back to you by …” — when you do not know yet. Her own reply can be short, for example “I'm not sure. I'll check and send you an email tomorrow.”
6.support: Cover the second reply and ask about the first only.
6.challenge: Ask for a reply that also says who she will check with.
6.monitoring: Whether her own reply includes a next step and a time.
6.evidence: Her own reply, in her words.
6.transition: Move on when she has given one reply of her own.

7.goal: To choose the best reply to four meeting questions, and to say the replies out loud.
7.interaction: S says her answers and you mark them on screen, then T–S, spoken.
run: For each of the four questions, she says the reply and you choose it on screen. Then press Check.
Go through the answers. On each wrong one, ask what the team would still not know.
Then ask the four questions yourself, in a different order, and let her answer out loud without reading.
exact: Asking out loud: “Do you need anything from us?” … “How much does a new laptop cost?” … “Is the new system on all the laptops?” … “Are we on track for Thursday?”
7.expected: “Is the new system on all the laptops?” — “Yes, on nineteen. One still has a problem with the screen.” · “Are we on track for Thursday?” — “Yes, we are on track, but I need the supplier to answer today.” · “How much does a new laptop cost?” — “I don't have the price. I will check and get back to you by tomorrow.” · “Do you need anything from us?” — “Yes. I need Ryan to call the supplier this week.” Spoken answers with other words are correct when they give the same information.
7.support: If she reads the reply, ask the question again and cover the screen.
7.challenge: Ask a fifth question that is not on the screen: “Who is going to tell the sales team?”
7.monitoring: Whether she can answer without reading, and whether the “I'll check” reply includes a time.
7.evidence: Which items were wrong at first, and how many spoken replies came without reading.
7.transition: Move on when she has answered the four questions out loud.

8.goal: To give the update again in the check-in, with the parts in place, and to answer questions, including one she cannot answer.
8.interaction: Role-play. You are Paula and the team; she gives her update.
run: She uses the same option as on screen 3.
Let her give the update without interruption. The sentence starters stay closed unless she stops.
Ask the three questions below for her option. The third has no answer she can know.
Write down one sentence as she said it, for screen 10.
exact: Option A: “Is the new system working?” … “Do you need anything from the team?” … “How much will a new laptop cost us?”
Option B: “What is the next step?” … “Do you need anything from the team?” … “Will it cost more than we planned?”
8.expected: An update with the three parts — where the work is, what comes next, what she needs — and answers to the three questions. For option A the facts are: nineteen laptops work, one has a screen problem, the next step is a new laptop from the supplier, Ryan needs to call the supplier. For the third question a complete reply is like “I don't have the price. I'll check with Ryan and get back to you tomorrow.”
8.support: If she stops, point at the next item on the list before you open the starters.
8.challenge: Interrupt once in the middle with “Sorry, when?”, and let her answer and go back.
8.monitoring: Which parts appear compared with screen 3, and what she does with the third question.
8.evidence: Her update on this screen, compared with screen 3, and one sentence written word for word.
8.transition: Move on when she has given the update and answered the three questions.

9.goal: To keep the interaction going after the update: answer one more question, ask the team one question, and check the answer.
9.interaction: T–S, unscripted. You are still the team.
run: Ask the question below.
Then invite her to ask the team one question. Give an answer with one detail that is not very clear, so she can check it.
exact: The question: “And what happens if the supplier doesn't answer this week?”
Handing the turn over: “OK. Any questions for the team?”
Your answer to her question, with an unclear detail: “Nora can look at it again on the… on Thursday, I think, or maybe Friday.”
9.expected: An answer with a reason or a next step, for example “Then I will call them again on Monday, because we need the laptop for the training.” Then one question from her, for example “Can Nora look at the screen again?”, and a check of your unclear answer, for example “So Nora can look at it on Thursday, right?”.
9.support: If she does not check the unclear detail, repeat it and ask: “Is that clear?”
9.challenge: Give a second unclear answer and see if she checks without being asked.
9.monitoring: Whether she asks a question and checks the unclear answer, using lesson 2.
9.evidence: Her question to the team, and whether she checked the unclear detail.
9.transition: Move on when she has asked one question and checked the answer.

10.goal: To compare her first update with the one she just gave, and to choose one sentence for the next round.
run: Write one thing that worked and one point to improve.
Write her update from screen 3 in the third box, as you noted it.
Build with her, in the fourth box, the version she will use next time, taking what worked on screen 8.
Read the box on screen and ask her to choose one sentence from the fourth box.
exact: Choosing the sentence: “Which sentence from this box do you want to use in the next round?”
10.expected: The difference between the two versions is the record of the block. A typical change is from a short status to three parts, and from “I don't know” to “I'll check and get back to you by …”. The fourth box holds her own words, improved, not the colleague's model copied word for word.
10.support: If she does not see the difference, read the two boxes aloud one after the other.
10.challenge: Ask what she would add for a meeting at her real work.
10.monitoring: Whether she can say what changed between the two versions.
10.evidence: The two versions, and the sentence she chose.
10.transition: Move on when she has chosen a sentence.

11.goal: To give the update in a new situation: Paula asks for the work two days earlier and asks something she cannot know, and she decides what is possible.
11.interaction: Role-play, new task. You are Paula.
run: Read the task and the list with her.
Let her start with the sentence from the fourth box.
After her update, ask for the date change, and then the question she cannot answer.
The sentence starters stay closed unless she stops.
exact: The change, option A: “We need all twenty laptops by Tuesday, not Thursday. Is that possible?”
The change, option B: “We need this two days earlier. Can you do that?”
The question she cannot answer: “Can the supplier send the laptop this week?”
11.expected: Her update, then a decision about the date that says what is possible and what is not, for example “I can have nineteen by Tuesday, but the last one depends on the supplier.”, then a reply to the last question with a next step and a time: “I'm not sure. I'll call the supplier today and get back to you.” This is a new task: the operation changed (a decision under a new condition), so compare it with screen 8 for what stayed and what was added.
11.support: If she accepts the new date without thinking, ask: “Are you sure? What about the last laptop?”
11.challenge: Push back once: “Tuesday is important. What can you do?” and let her offer an option.
11.monitoring: Whether she says what is possible and what is not, and whether the sentence from the fourth box appears.
11.evidence: Her decision about the date, her reply to the last question, and whether the point to improve changed.
11.transition: Move on when she has given the update, the decision and the reply.

12.goal: To close the lesson and the block: what was worked on, how confident she feels, and the homework said out loud.
12.interaction: T–S, going through the recap and the confidence scale together.
run: Go through the recap list with her.
Let her fill the confidence scale herself.
Read the three lines on the right and say the homework out loud.
exact: The homework, said out loud: “This week, in a meeting, when you do not know an answer, say when you will check.”
12.expected: The recap has six lines: giving an update before any model, comparing it with a colleague's, replies that keep a meeting moving, the parts of a short update, the update with questions, and the update again with a change of date. The confidence scale is hers. This is the last lesson of the block: note in the post-lesson record what the four lessons showed about her explanations, her questions and the meetings she described.
12.support: If she marks everything low, read the sentence she chose from the fourth box.
12.challenge: Ask which meeting this week she will use the update in.
12.monitoring: Whether her self-assessment matches what you observed in the block.
12.evidence: Her confidence marks, and the meeting she names.
12.transition: End here. The next lessons are planned from what this block showed.
